Formal Semantics for Agentic Tool Protocols:
A Process Calculus Approach

Andreas Schlapbach Note: © 2026 Andreas Schlapbach. Licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Research supported by SBB-IT. The views expressed in this paper are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect the views or policies of SBB. ORCID: 0009-0006-2329-2626. Affiliation: SBB (Swiss Federal Railways), SBB IT, Bern, Switzerland
schlpbch@gmail.com
Abstract

The emergence of large language model agents capable of invoking external tools has created urgent need for formal verification of agent protocols. Two paradigms dominate this space: Schema-Guided Dialogue (SGD), a research framework for zero-shot API generalization, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an industry standard for agent–tool integration. While both enable dynamic service discovery through schema descriptions, their formal relationship remains unexplored. Building on prior work establishing the conceptual convergence of these paradigms (Schlapbach, 2026), we present the first process calculus formalization of SGD and MCP, proving they are structurally bisimilar under a well-defined mapping Φ\Phi. However, we demonstrate that the reverse mapping Φ−1\Phi^{-1} is partial and lossy, revealing critical gaps in MCP’s expressivity. Through bidirectional analysis, we identify five principles—semantic completeness, explicit action boundaries, failure mode documentation, progressive disclosure compatibility, and inter-tool relationship declaration—as necessary and sufficient conditions for full behavioral equivalence. We formalize these principles as type-system extensions 𝖬𝖢𝖯+\mathsf{MCP}^{+}, proving 𝖬𝖢𝖯+≅𝖲𝖦𝖣\mathsf{MCP}^{+}\cong\mathsf{SGD}. Our work provides the first formal foundation for verified agent systems and establishes schema quality as a provable safety property.

Keywords: Process calculus, bisimulation, schema-guided dialogue, model context protocol, agent verification, type safety.

1 Introduction

The rapid deployment of large language model (LLM) agents (Vaswani et al., 2017; Brown et al., 2020) in production systems has created a critical gap: while these agents—capable of multi-step reasoning (Wei et al., 2022) and reactive tool use (Yao et al., 2023)—orchestrate complex workflows across multiple services, we lack formal methods to verify their correctness, safety, and behavioral properties. Two paradigms have emerged to address agent–tool integration:

  1. 1.

    Schema-Guided Dialogue (SGD) (Rastogi et al., 2020): A research framework demonstrating that dialogue models can generalize zero-shot to new APIs when provided natural-language schema descriptions at runtime.

  2. 2.

    Model Context Protocol (MCP) (Anthropic, 2025): An industry standard introduced by Anthropic to solve the N-to-M integration problem, enabling any LLM host to connect with any compliant server through standardized primitives.

Both paradigms share a core principle: agents discover and reason about services through machine-readable schemas without retraining. Schlapbach (2026) established that SGD and MCP converge conceptually around five schema design principles, demonstrating empirical improvements in agent routing accuracy. However, the formal relationship between the two protocols remains unexplored. Can we prove they are equivalent? What properties are preserved under transformation? What gaps exist in either framework? This paper provides rigorous answers by grounding the analysis in process calculus.

1.1 Contributions

This paper makes the following contributions:

  1. 1.

    First formal semantics for SGD and MCP using π​-calculus\pi\text{-calculus}, defining their syntax, operational semantics, and labeled transition systems (Section 3).

  2. 2.

    Bisimulation proof showing 𝖲𝖦𝖣∼𝖬𝖢𝖯\mathsf{SGD}\sim\mathsf{MCP} under mapping Φ\Phi, establishing structural and behavioral equivalence (Section 4).

  3. 3.

    Reverse mapping analysis proving Φ−1\Phi^{-1} is partial and lossy, revealing gaps in MCP’s metadata model (Section 5).

  4. 4.

    Five principles as type system formalizing necessary conditions for agent safety and schema quality (Section 6).

  5. 5.

    Extended calculus 𝖬𝖢𝖯+\mathsf{MCP}^{+} proving that adding five principles creates full bijection: 𝖬𝖢𝖯+≅𝖲𝖦𝖣\mathsf{MCP}^{+}\cong\mathsf{SGD} (Section 7).

  6. 6.

    Security properties as process invariants, including capability confinement and tool-poisoning prevention (Section 8).

1.2 Motivation: Why Formal Semantics Matter

Consider a banking agent orchestrating account transfers:

  1. 1.

    𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗂𝖿𝗒​_​𝖻𝖺𝗅𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾​(𝑎𝑐𝑐𝑜𝑢𝑛𝑡​_​𝑖𝑑)→𝑏𝑎𝑙𝑎𝑛𝑐𝑒\mathsf{verify\_balance}(\mathit{account\_id})\to\mathit{balance}

  2. 2.

    𝗏𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖽𝖺𝗍𝖾​_​𝗍𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌𝖿𝖾𝗋​(𝑎𝑚𝑜𝑢𝑛𝑡,𝑏𝑎𝑙𝑎𝑛𝑐𝑒)→𝑎𝑢𝑡ℎ𝑜𝑟𝑖𝑧𝑒𝑑\mathsf{validate\_transfer}(\mathit{amount},\,\mathit{balance})\to\mathit{authorized}

  3. 3.

    𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾​_​𝗍𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌𝖿𝖾𝗋​(𝑓𝑟𝑜𝑚,𝑡𝑜,𝑎𝑚𝑜𝑢𝑛𝑡)→𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑓𝑖𝑟𝑚𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛\mathsf{execute\_transfer}(\mathit{from},\,\mathit{to},\,\mathit{amount})\to\mathit{confirmation}

Questions requiring formal answers include: Does the agent always check balance before transfer? Can step 3 execute without step 2 approval? What happens if step 3 fails after debiting the account? Can we prove properties of agent1∣agent2\text{agent}_{1}\mathbin{\mid}\text{agent}_{2}?

Current approaches rely on testing (incomplete coverage), prompt engineering (Wei et al., 2022) (no guarantees, brittle), or human review (not scalable). Agent frameworks grounded in BDI theory (Rao and Georgeff, 1995) offer structured reasoning, but stop short of protocol-level verification. Formal semantics enable verification (prove safety for all executions), composition (build complex systems from verified components), optimization (preserve equivalence under transformation), and debugging (trace violations to specific protocol violations).

2 Background and Related Work

2.1 Process Calculi for Concurrency

Process calculi provide mathematical frameworks for reasoning about concurrent, communicating systems. The π​-calculus\pi\text{-calculus} (Milner, 1999) extends CCS (Milner, 1989) with mobile channels, enabling dynamic network topologies—essential for agent systems where tool availability changes at runtime.

Key concepts.

Processes are computational entities that evolve through transitions; channels are communication primitives for message passing; operators include parallel composition (∣)(\mathbin{\mid}), restriction (ν)(\nu), and replication (!⋅)(!{\cdot}); bisimulation is a behavioral equivalence relation preserving observations.

Related work includes session types (Honda et al., 1998) for protocol verification, choreography calculi (Carbone et al., 2012) for multi-party workflows, and probabilistic process algebras (D’Argenio and others, 2022) for stochastic systems. Foundational correctness arguments for concurrent programs trace back to Lamport (Lamport, 1977). However, all these frameworks assume static protocols. Agent systems require runtime schema interpretation.

2.2 Schema-Guided Dialogue Systems

The SGD dataset (Rastogi et al., 2020) introduced a paradigm shift in task-oriented dialogue: rather than training on fixed ontologies, SGD models learn to interpret arbitrary API schemas at runtime. Key components are intents (high-level user goals), slots (parameters to collect), schemas (JSON definitions with natural-language descriptions), and state tracking (frame-based representation across turns). Dialogue state tracking has a longer history in shared tasks (Williams et al., 2016), and BERT-based encoders (Devlin et al., 2019) enabled strong cross-service generalisation. Fast and robust SGD trackers (Gupta et al., 2020) demonstrated practical viability at scale. More recently, in-context learning has shown that few demonstration examples suffice to adapt to new schemas—mirroring the zero-shot generalisation that SGD pioneered.

2.3 Model Context Protocol

MCP (Anthropic, 2025) standardizes agent–tool communication through three primitives: Tools (executable functions), Resources (read-only context), and Prompts (reusable workflow templates). The architecture comprises a host (LLM environment), a client (protocol handler), and a server (service exposing primitives via JSON-RPC 2.0). Schemas are expressed in OpenAPI/JSON Schema (Foundation, 2021), distinguishing MCP from alternative API paradigms such as gRPC (Google, 2015) and GraphQL (Facebook, 2015). Active tool discovery at runtime—where agents autonomously locate and load new servers—is explored by MCP-Zero (Gao et al., 2025).

2.4 Formal Methods for Agent Systems

Recent work applies formal methods to LLM agents: LMQL (Beurer-Kellner et al., 2023) constrains outputs via formal grammars; ToolEmu (Patil et al., 2024) tests tool-use agents with emulated environments; MCPBench (Chen et al., 2025) benchmarks MCP tool selection; PARSE (Shrimal et al., 2025) applies LLM-driven schema optimisation for reliable entity extraction; and PromptBench (Zhu et al., 2024) evaluates LLM robustness under adversarial prompts. Formal verification of neural components has been approached via SMT solving (Katz et al., 2017) and certified defences (Wong and Kolter, 2018). Safe reinforcement learning (García and Fernández, 2015) provides constrained optimisation guarantees orthogonal to our protocol-level approach. Weighted majority voting (Xie et al., 2026) has been applied to improve LLM decision reliability under uncertainty. None of these works provide process calculus semantics for agent–tool protocols.

3 Process Calculus Formalization

We formalize SGD and MCP as communicating processes in π​-calculus\pi\text{-calculus}, defining their syntax, operational semantics, and observable behaviors.

3.1 SGD Process Calculus

Syntax.

The set of SGD processes is defined by the following grammar, where nn is a name (string), dd a natural-language description, RR a list of required slots, OO a list of optional slots, and t∈{𝗍𝗋𝗎𝖾,𝖿𝖺𝗅𝗌𝖾}t\in\{\mathsf{true},\mathsf{false}\} a transactionality flag:

S::=\displaystyle S\;::=\; 𝖨𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗇𝗍​⟨n,d,R,O,t⟩\displaystyle\mathsf{Intent}\langle n,\,d,\,R,\,O,\,t\rangle intent with metadata
∣\displaystyle\mid\; 𝖲𝗅𝗈𝗍​⟨𝑛𝑎𝑚𝑒,𝑡𝑦𝑝𝑒,𝑣𝑎𝑙𝑠⟩\displaystyle\mathsf{Slot}\langle\mathit{name},\,\mathit{type},\,\mathit{vals}\rangle slot definition
∣\displaystyle\mid\; 𝖢𝗈𝗅𝗅𝖾𝖼𝗍𝖲𝗅𝗈𝗍​⟨s,v⟩.S\displaystyle\mathsf{CollectSlot}\langle s,\,v\rangle\mathbin{.}S slot collection, then SS
∣\displaystyle\mid\; 𝖤𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾​⟨𝑖𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑡,𝑏𝑖𝑛𝑑𝑖𝑛𝑔𝑠⟩\displaystyle\mathsf{Execute}\langle\mathit{intent},\,\mathit{bindings}\rangle API invocation
∣\displaystyle\mid\; 𝖱𝖾𝗌𝗎𝗅𝗍​⟨𝑜𝑢𝑡𝑝𝑢𝑡⟩\displaystyle\mathsf{Result}\langle\mathit{output}\rangle return value
∣\displaystyle\mid\; 𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋​⟨𝑡𝑦𝑝𝑒,𝑚𝑠𝑔⟩\displaystyle\mathsf{Error}\langle\mathit{type},\,\mathit{msg}\rangle error state
∣\displaystyle\mid\; S1∣S2\displaystyle S_{1}\mathbin{\mid}S_{2} parallel composition
∣\displaystyle\mid\; (ν​c)​S\displaystyle(\nu\,c)\;S channel restriction
∣\displaystyle\mid\; !S\displaystyle{!}S replication
∣\displaystyle\mid\; 𝟎\displaystyle\mathbf{0} null process

Operational Semantics.

The transition rules for SGD processes are given in Figure 1.

Example.

⬇
BookFlight = Intent⟨\langle
name = "BookFlight",
description = "Books a flight reservation",
R = [Slot⟨\langle"origin", "string", airports⟩\rangle,
Slot⟨\langle"destination", "string", airports⟩\rangle,
Slot⟨\langle"date", "date", []⟩\rangle],
O = [Slot⟨\langle"class", "string", ["economy", "business"]⟩\rangle],
t = true // Transaction requires confirmation
⟩\rangle
// Execution trace:
BookFlight
--invoke("BookFlight", {origin: "ZRH", destination: "JFK", date: "2026-03-15"})⟶\longrightarrow
Execute⟨\langle"BookFlight", {origin: "ZRH", ...}⟩\rangle
--execute (with approval)⟶\longrightarrow
Result⟨\langle{confirmation: "ABC123"}⟩\rangle

3.2 MCP Process Calculus

Syntax.

The set of MCP processes is defined by the following grammar, where 𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎\mathit{schema} is a JSON Schema object, 𝑐𝑎𝑝𝑠\mathit{caps} a capability set, and 𝑢𝑟𝑖\mathit{uri} a resource identifier:

M::=\displaystyle M\;::=\; 𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅​⟨n,d,𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎⟩\displaystyle\mathsf{Tool}\langle n,\,d,\,\mathit{schema}\rangle tool definition
∣\displaystyle\mid\; 𝖱𝖾𝗌𝗈𝗎𝗋𝖼𝖾​⟨𝑢𝑟𝑖,𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑡⟩\displaystyle\mathsf{Resource}\langle\mathit{uri},\,\mathit{content}\rangle read-only resource
∣\displaystyle\mid\; 𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗆𝗉𝗍​⟨𝑡𝑒𝑚𝑝𝑙𝑎𝑡𝑒,𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑠⟩\displaystyle\mathsf{Prompt}\langle\mathit{template},\,\mathit{args}\rangle workflow template
∣\displaystyle\mid\; 𝖨𝗇𝗂𝗍𝗂𝖺𝗅𝗂𝗓𝖾​⟨𝑐𝑎𝑝𝑠⟩\displaystyle\mathsf{Initialize}\langle\mathit{caps}\rangle capability negotiation
∣\displaystyle\mid\; 𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅𝗌𝖫𝗂𝗌𝗍​⟨𝑚𝑒𝑡𝑎𝑑𝑎𝑡𝑎⟩\displaystyle\mathsf{ToolsList}\langle\mathit{metadata}\rangle discovery response
∣\displaystyle\mid\; 𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅𝖢𝖺𝗅𝗅​⟨n,𝑝𝑎𝑟𝑎𝑚𝑠⟩\displaystyle\mathsf{ToolCall}\langle n,\,\mathit{params}\rangle tool invocation
∣\displaystyle\mid\; 𝖵𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖽𝖺𝗍𝖾​⟨𝑝𝑎𝑟𝑎𝑚𝑠,𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎⟩\displaystyle\mathsf{Validate}\langle\mathit{params},\,\mathit{schema}\rangle parameter validation
∣\displaystyle\mid\; 𝖱𝖾𝗌𝗎𝗅𝗍​⟨𝑜𝑢𝑡𝑝𝑢𝑡⟩\displaystyle\mathsf{Result}\langle\mathit{output}\rangle return value
∣\displaystyle\mid\; 𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋​⟨𝑡𝑦𝑝𝑒,𝑚𝑠𝑔⟩\displaystyle\mathsf{Error}\langle\mathit{type},\,\mathit{msg}\rangle error state
∣\displaystyle\mid\; M1∣M2\displaystyle M_{1}\mathbin{\mid}M_{2} parallel composition
∣\displaystyle\mid\; (ν​c)​M\displaystyle(\nu\,c)\;M channel restriction
∣\displaystyle\mid\; !M\displaystyle{!}M replication
∣\displaystyle\mid\; 𝟎\displaystyle\mathbf{0} null process

Operational Semantics.

The transition rules for MCP processes are given in Figure 2.

Example.

⬇
GitHubCreateIssue = Tool⟨\langle
name = "create_issue",
description = "Creates a new GitHub issue in a repository",
schema = {
"type": "object",
"required": ["owner", "repo", "title"],
"properties": {
"owner": {"type": "string", "description": "Repository owner"},
"repo": {"type": "string", "description": "Repository name"},
"title": {"type": "string", "description": "Issue title"},
"body": {"type": "string", "description": "Issue description"}
}
}
⟩\rangle
// Execution trace:
GitHubCreateIssue
--call("create_issue", {owner: "anthropic", repo: "mcp", title: "Bug"})⟶\longrightarrow
Validate⟨\langle{owner: "anthropic", ...}, schema⟩\rangle
--validate (success)⟶\longrightarrow
Execute⟨\langle"create_issue", {owner: "anthropic", ...}⟩\rangle
--execute⟶\longrightarrow
Result⟨\langle{issue_number: 42, url: "https://..."}⟩\rangle

3.3 Labeled Transition Systems

Definition 3.1 (SGD LTS).

The labeled transition system for 𝖲𝖦𝖣\mathsf{SGD} is the tuple (𝑆𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑠𝖲𝖦𝖣,𝐿𝑎𝑏𝑒𝑙𝑠𝖲𝖦𝖣,→𝖲𝖦𝖣)(\mathit{States}_{\mathsf{SGD}},\,\mathit{Labels}_{\mathsf{SGD}},\,\to_{\mathsf{SGD}}) where:

𝑆𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑠𝖲𝖦𝖣\displaystyle\mathit{States}_{\mathsf{SGD}} ={S∣S​ is a well-formed SGD process}\displaystyle=\{S\mid S\text{ is a well-formed SGD process}\}
𝐿𝑎𝑏𝑒𝑙𝑠𝖲𝖦𝖣\displaystyle\mathit{Labels}_{\mathsf{SGD}} ={𝗂𝗇𝗏𝗈𝗄𝖾⁡(n,p),𝖼𝗈𝗅𝗅𝖾𝖼𝗍⁡(s,v),𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾,𝗋𝖾𝗌𝗎𝗅𝗍⁡(o),𝖾𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋⁡(t,m)}\displaystyle=\{\mathsf{invoke}(n,\,p),\;\mathsf{collect}(s,v),\;\mathsf{execute},\;\mathsf{result}(o),\;\mathsf{error}(t,\,m)\}
→𝖲𝖦𝖣\displaystyle\to_{\mathsf{SGD}} ⊆𝑆𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑠𝖲𝖦𝖣×𝐿𝑎𝑏𝑒𝑙𝑠𝖲𝖦𝖣×𝑆𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑠𝖲𝖦𝖣\displaystyle\;\subseteq\;\mathit{States}_{\mathsf{SGD}}\times\mathit{Labels}_{\mathsf{SGD}}\times\mathit{States}_{\mathsf{SGD}}
Definition 3.2 (MCP LTS).

The labeled transition system for 𝖬𝖢𝖯\mathsf{MCP} is the tuple (𝑆𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑠𝖬𝖢𝖯,𝐿𝑎𝑏𝑒𝑙𝑠𝖬𝖢𝖯,→𝖬𝖢𝖯)(\mathit{States}_{\mathsf{MCP}},\,\mathit{Labels}_{\mathsf{MCP}},\,\to_{\mathsf{MCP}}) where:

𝑆𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑠𝖬𝖢𝖯\displaystyle\mathit{States}_{\mathsf{MCP}} ={M∣M​ is a well-formed MCP process}\displaystyle=\{M\mid M\text{ is a well-formed MCP process}\}
𝐿𝑎𝑏𝑒𝑙𝑠𝖬𝖢𝖯\displaystyle\mathit{Labels}_{\mathsf{MCP}} ={𝖼𝖺𝗅𝗅⁡(n,p),τ,𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾,𝗋𝖾𝗌𝗎𝗅𝗍⁡(o),𝖾𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋⁡(t,m),𝗋𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(u)}\displaystyle=\{\mathsf{call}(n,\,p),\;\tau,\;\mathsf{execute},\;\mathsf{result}(o),\;\mathsf{error}(t,\,m),\;\mathsf{read}(u)\}
→𝖬𝖢𝖯\displaystyle\to_{\mathsf{MCP}} ⊆𝑆𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑠𝖬𝖢𝖯×𝐿𝑎𝑏𝑒𝑙𝑠𝖬𝖢𝖯×𝑆𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑠𝖬𝖢𝖯\displaystyle\;\subseteq\;\mathit{States}_{\mathsf{MCP}}\times\mathit{Labels}_{\mathsf{MCP}}\times\mathit{States}_{\mathsf{MCP}}

Silent (τ\tau) actions: 𝖼𝗈𝗅𝗅𝖾𝖼𝗍​_​𝗌𝗅𝗈𝗍\mathsf{collect\_slot}, 𝗏𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖽𝖺𝗍𝖾\mathsf{validate}, 𝗇𝖾𝗀𝗈𝗍𝗂𝖺𝗍𝖾\mathsf{negotiate}. Observable actions: 𝗂𝗇𝗏𝗈𝗄𝖾/𝖼𝖺𝗅𝗅\mathsf{invoke/call}, 𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾\mathsf{execute}, 𝗋𝖾𝗌𝗎𝗅𝗍⁡(⋅)\mathsf{result}(\cdot), 𝖾𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋⁡(⋅,⋅)\mathsf{error}(\cdot,\,\cdot), 𝗋𝖾𝖺𝖽⁡(⋅)\mathsf{read}(\cdot).

4 Forward Bisimulation: 𝖲𝖦𝖣→𝖬𝖢𝖯\mathsf{SGD}\to\mathsf{MCP}

4.1 Mapping Function Φ\Phi

Definition 4.1 (Schema Mapping Φ:𝖲𝖦𝖣→𝖬𝖢𝖯\Phi:\mathsf{SGD}\to\mathsf{MCP}).
Φ⁡(𝖨𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗇𝗍⁡⟨n,d,R,O,t⟩)\displaystyle\Phi\!\left(\mathsf{Intent}\langle n,\,d,\,R,\,O,\,t\rangle\right) =𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅​⟨n,d,𝗌𝖼𝗁𝖾𝗆𝖺⁡(R,O)⟩\displaystyle\;=\;\mathsf{Tool}\langle n,\,d,\,\mathsf{schema}(R,O)\rangle
where𝗌𝖼𝗁𝖾𝗆𝖺⁡(R,O)\displaystyle\text{where}\quad\mathsf{schema}(R,O) ={"𝚝𝚢𝚙𝚎":"𝚘𝚋𝚓𝚎𝚌𝚝","𝚛𝚎𝚚𝚞𝚒𝚛𝚎𝚍":[s.𝑛𝑎𝑚𝑒∣s∈R],\displaystyle\;=\;\Bigl\{\mathtt{"type"}{:}\;\mathtt{"object"},\;\mathtt{"required"}{:}\;[s.\mathit{name}\mid s\in R],
"𝚙𝚛𝚘𝚙𝚎𝚛𝚝𝚒𝚎𝚜":{s.𝑛𝑎𝑚𝑒:𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗉(s)∣s∈R∪O}}\displaystyle\quad\quad\quad\mathtt{"properties"}{:}\;\{s.\mathit{name}:\mathsf{prop}(s)\mid s\in R\cup O\}\Bigr\}
𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗉⁡(s)\displaystyle\mathsf{prop}(s) ={"𝚝𝚢𝚙𝚎":s.𝑡𝑦𝑝𝑒,"𝚍𝚎𝚜𝚌𝚛𝚒𝚙𝚝𝚒𝚘𝚗":s.𝑑𝑒𝑠𝑐}∪({"𝚎𝚗𝚞𝚖":s.𝑣𝑎𝑙𝑠} if s.𝑣𝑎𝑙𝑠≠∅)\displaystyle\;=\;\{\mathtt{"type"}{:}\;s.\mathit{type},\;\mathtt{"description"}{:}\;s.\mathit{desc}\}\cup(\{\mathtt{"enum"}{:}\;s.\mathit{vals}\}\text{ if }s.\mathit{vals}\neq\emptyset)
Φ⁡(𝖤𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾​⟨n,𝑏𝑖𝑛𝑑𝑖𝑛𝑔𝑠⟩)\displaystyle\Phi\!\left(\mathsf{Execute}\langle n,\,\mathit{bindings}\rangle\right) =𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅𝖢𝖺𝗅𝗅⟨n,𝖩𝖲𝖮𝖭.𝖾𝗇𝖼𝗈𝖽𝖾(𝑏𝑖𝑛𝑑𝑖𝑛𝑔𝑠)⟩\displaystyle\;=\;\mathsf{ToolCall}\langle n,\,\mathsf{JSON.encode}(\mathit{bindings})\rangle
Φ⁡(𝖱𝖾𝗌𝗎𝗅𝗍​⟨o⟩)\displaystyle\Phi\!\left(\mathsf{Result}\langle o\rangle\right) =𝖱𝖾𝗌𝗎𝗅𝗍​⟨o⟩\displaystyle\;=\;\mathsf{Result}\langle o\rangle
Φ⁡(𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋​⟨t,m⟩)\displaystyle\Phi\!\left(\mathsf{Error}\langle t,\,m\rangle\right) =𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋​⟨t,m⟩\displaystyle\;=\;\mathsf{Error}\langle t,\,m\rangle
Φ⁡(S1∣S2)\displaystyle\Phi(S_{1}\mathbin{\mid}S_{2}) =Φ⁡(S1)∣Φ⁡(S2)\displaystyle\;=\;\Phi(S_{1})\mathbin{\mid}\Phi(S_{2})
Φ⁡((ν​c)​S)\displaystyle\Phi((\nu\,c)\;S) =(ν​c)​Φ​(S)\displaystyle\;=\;(\nu\,c)\;\Phi(S)
Φ(!S)\displaystyle\Phi({!}S) =!Φ(S)\displaystyle\;=\;{!}\Phi(S)
Φ⁡(𝟎)\displaystyle\Phi(\mathbf{0}) = 0\displaystyle\;=\;\mathbf{0}

true

4.2 Action Equivalence

Definition 4.2 (Action Equivalence ≈\approx).
𝗂𝗇𝗏𝗈𝗄𝖾⁡(n,p)≈𝖼𝖺𝗅𝗅⁡(n,p),𝖼𝗈𝗅𝗅𝖾𝖼𝗍⁡(s,v)≈τ,𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾≈𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾,𝗋𝖾𝗌𝗎𝗅𝗍⁡(o)≈𝗋𝖾𝗌𝗎𝗅𝗍⁡(o),𝖾𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋⁡(t,m)≈𝖾𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋⁡(t,m)\mathsf{invoke}(n,\,p)\approx\mathsf{call}(n,\,p),\mathsf{collect}(s,v)\approx\tau,\mathsf{execute}\approx\mathsf{execute},\mathsf{result}(o)\approx\mathsf{result}(o),\mathsf{error}(t,\,m)\approx\mathsf{error}(t,\,m)

4.3 Bisimulation and Main Theorem

Definition 4.3 (Strong Bisimulation).

A symmetric relation ℛ⊆𝑆𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑠𝖲𝖦𝖣×𝑆𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑠𝖬𝖢𝖯\mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathit{States}_{\mathsf{SGD}}\times\mathit{States}_{\mathsf{MCP}} is a strong bisimulation iff whenever (S,M)∈ℛ(S,M)\in\mathcal{R}:

  1. 1.

    Forward: if S→𝛼S′S\xrightarrow{\alpha}S^{\prime} then ∃M′,β.M→𝛽M′\exists M^{\prime},\beta.\;M\xrightarrow{\beta}M^{\prime} and α≈β\alpha\approx\beta and (S′,M′)∈ℛ(S^{\prime},M^{\prime})\in\mathcal{R}.

  2. 2.

    Backward: if M→𝛽M′M\xrightarrow{\beta}M^{\prime} then ∃S′,α.S→𝛼S′\exists S^{\prime},\alpha.\;S\xrightarrow{\alpha}S^{\prime} and α≈β\alpha\approx\beta and (S′,M′)∈ℛ(S^{\prime},M^{\prime})\in\mathcal{R}.

We write S∼MS\sim M iff there exists a bisimulation ℛ\mathcal{R} with (S,M)∈ℛ(S,M)\in\mathcal{R}.

Theorem 4.4 (𝖲𝖦𝖣∼𝖬𝖢𝖯\mathsf{SGD}\sim\mathsf{MCP} under Φ\Phi).

∀S∈𝖲𝖦𝖣.S∼Φ⁡(S)\forall S\in\mathsf{SGD}.\;S\sim\Phi(S).

Proof.

Define ℛ={(S,Φ⁡(S))∣S∈𝖲𝖦𝖣}\mathcal{R}=\{(S,\Phi(S))\mid S\in\mathsf{SGD}\}. We prove ℛ\mathcal{R} is a bisimulation by structural induction.

Lemma 4.5 (Intent ∼\sim Tool).

𝖨𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗇𝗍⁡⟨n,d,R,O,t⟩∼𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅⁡⟨n,d,𝗌𝖼𝗁𝖾𝗆𝖺⁡(R,O)⟩\mathsf{Intent}\langle n,\,d,\,R,\,O,\,t\rangle\;\sim\;\mathsf{Tool}\langle n,\,d,\,\mathsf{schema}(R,O)\rangle.

Proof.

Suppose 𝖨𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗇𝗍⁡⟨n,d,R,O,t⟩→𝗂𝗇𝗏𝗈𝗄𝖾⁡(n,p)S′\mathsf{Intent}\langle n,\,d,\,R,\,O,\,t\rangle\xrightarrow{\mathsf{invoke}(n,\,p)}S^{\prime}.

Case 1: pp satisfies all slots in RR. Then S′=𝖤𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾​⟨n,p⟩S^{\prime}=\mathsf{Execute}\langle n,\,p\rangle. For the tool:

𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅⁡⟨n,d,𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎⟩→𝖼𝖺𝗅𝗅⁡(n,p)𝖵𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖽𝖺𝗍𝖾⁡⟨p,𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎⟩→𝜏𝖤𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾⁡⟨n,p⟩\mathsf{Tool}\langle n,\,d,\,\mathit{schema}\rangle\;\xrightarrow{\mathsf{call}(n,\,p)}\;\mathsf{Validate}\langle p,\,\mathit{schema}\rangle\;\xrightarrow{\tau}\;\mathsf{Execute}\langle n,\,p\rangle

Since 𝗌𝖼𝗁𝖾𝗆𝖺(R,O).𝚛𝚎𝚚𝚞𝚒𝚛𝚎𝚍=[s.𝑛𝑎𝑚𝑒∣s∈R]\mathsf{schema}(R,O).\mathtt{required}=[s.\mathit{name}\mid s\in R], validation succeeds iff pp satisfies RR. By definition, 𝖤𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾⁡⟨n,p⟩∼𝖤𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾⁡⟨n,p⟩\mathsf{Execute}\langle n,\,p\rangle\sim\mathsf{Execute}\langle n,\,p\rangle. ✓

Case 2: pp missing required slots. Then S′=𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋⁡⟨𝖬𝗂𝗌𝗌𝗂𝗇𝗀𝖲𝗅𝗈𝗍𝗌,R∖p⟩S^{\prime}=\mathsf{Error}\langle\mathsf{MissingSlots},\,R\setminus p\rangle. The tool produces 𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋​⟨𝖵𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖽𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋,R∖p⟩\mathsf{Error}\langle\mathsf{ValidationError},\,R\setminus p\rangle via the MCP-Validate-Err rule; error terms are observationally equivalent. ✓

The backward direction is symmetric by construction of Φ\Phi. ∎

Lemma 4.6 (Execution Preservation).

𝖤𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾⟨n,𝑏𝑖𝑛𝑑𝑖𝑛𝑔𝑠⟩𝖲𝖦𝖣∼𝖤𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾⟨n,𝖩𝖲𝖮𝖭.𝖾𝗇𝖼𝗈𝖽𝖾(𝑏𝑖𝑛𝑑𝑖𝑛𝑔𝑠)⟩𝖬𝖢𝖯\mathsf{Execute}\langle n,\,\mathit{bindings}\rangle_{\mathsf{SGD}}\;\sim\;\mathsf{Execute}\langle n,\,\mathsf{JSON.encode}(\mathit{bindings})\rangle_{\mathsf{MCP}}.

Proof.

Both processes transition via 𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾\mathsf{execute} to 𝖱𝖾𝗌𝗎𝗅𝗍​⟨𝑜𝑢𝑡𝑝𝑢𝑡⟩\mathsf{Result}\langle\mathit{output}\rangle where 𝑜𝑢𝑡𝑝𝑢𝑡=𝗂𝗇𝗏𝗈𝗄𝖾​_​𝖺𝗉𝗂​(n,𝑏𝑖𝑛𝑑𝑖𝑛𝑔𝑠)\mathit{output}=\mathsf{invoke\_api}(n,\mathit{bindings}). JSON encoding is a bijection on well-typed parameters, so 𝗂𝗇𝗏𝗈𝗄𝖾​_​𝖺𝗉𝗂​(n,b)=𝗂𝗇𝗏𝗈𝗄𝖾​_​𝖺𝗉𝗂​(n,𝖽𝖾𝖼𝗈𝖽𝖾⁡(𝖾𝗇𝖼𝗈𝖽𝖾⁡(b)))\mathsf{invoke\_api}(n,\mathit{b})=\mathsf{invoke\_api}(n,\mathsf{decode}(\mathsf{encode}(\mathit{b}))). ∎

Induction.

Base case (S=𝟎S=\mathbf{0}): Φ⁡(𝟎)=𝟎\Phi(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{0} and 𝟎∼𝟎\mathbf{0}\sim\mathbf{0} trivially.

Inductive case (S=S1∣S2S=S_{1}\mathbin{\mid}S_{2}): By IH, Si∼Φ⁡(Si)S_{i}\sim\Phi(S_{i}). If S1∣S2→𝛼S1′∣S2S_{1}\mathbin{\mid}S_{2}\xrightarrow{\alpha}S_{1}^{\prime}\mathbin{\mid}S_{2} then by IH Φ⁡(S1)→𝛽M1′\Phi(S_{1})\xrightarrow{\beta}M_{1}^{\prime} with S1′∼M1′S_{1}^{\prime}\sim M_{1}^{\prime} and α≈β\alpha\approx\beta, hence Φ⁡(S1)∣Φ⁡(S2)→𝛽M1′∣Φ⁡(S2)\Phi(S_{1})\mathbin{\mid}\Phi(S_{2})\xrightarrow{\beta}M_{1}^{\prime}\mathbin{\mid}\Phi(S_{2}), and (S1′∣S2)∼(M1′∣Φ⁡(S2))(S_{1}^{\prime}\mathbin{\mid}S_{2})\sim(M_{1}^{\prime}\mathbin{\mid}\Phi(S_{2})). The symmetric case for S2S_{2} is identical.

Inductive case (S=𝖨𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗇𝗍⁡⟨n,d,R,O,t⟩S=\mathsf{Intent}\langle n,\,d,\,R,\,O,\,t\rangle): By Lemma 4.5.

Inductive case (S=(ν​c)​S′S=(\nu\,c)\;S^{\prime}): Φ⁡((ν​c)​S′)=(ν​c)​Φ​(S′)\Phi((\nu\,c)\;S^{\prime})=(\nu\,c)\;\Phi(S^{\prime}). By IH, S′∼Φ⁡(S′)S^{\prime}\sim\Phi(S^{\prime}). Channel restriction preserves bisimulation (standard π​-calculus\pi\text{-calculus} result (Milner, 1999)). ∎

Corollary 4.7 (Trace Equivalence).

∀S∈𝖲𝖦𝖣,∀\forall S\in\mathsf{SGD},\;\forall trace tt:  SS can produce trace t⇔Φ⁡(S)t\iff\Phi(S) can produce trace Φ⁡(t)\Phi(t).

Corollary 4.8 (Zero-Shot Generalization Transfer).

If an SGD model handles 𝐼𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑡​I\mathit{Intent}\ I zero-shot via schema ss, then an MCP model handles 𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅​⟨⋅,⋅,Φ⁡(s)⟩\mathsf{Tool}\langle\cdot,\,\cdot,\,\Phi(s)\rangle zero-shot via Φ⁡(s)\Phi(s).

5 Reverse Mapping and Gap Analysis

5.1 Attempted Reverse Mapping

Definition 5.1 (Reverse Mapping Φ−1:𝖬𝖢𝖯⇀𝖲𝖦𝖣\Phi^{-1}:\mathsf{MCP}\rightharpoonup\mathsf{SGD}).
Φ−1​(𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅⁡⟨n,d,𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎⟩)\displaystyle\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\mathsf{Tool}\langle n,\,d,\,\mathit{schema}\rangle\right) =𝖨𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗇𝗍⁡⟨n,d,R⁡(𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎),O⁡(𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎),?⟩\displaystyle\;=\;\mathsf{Intent}\langle n,\,d,\,R(\mathit{schema}),\,O(\mathit{schema}),\,\;?\rangle
where ​R​(𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎)\displaystyle\text{where }\;R(\mathit{schema}) ={𝖲𝗅𝗈𝗍⟨x,𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎.𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑝[x],⟩∣x∈𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎.𝑟𝑒𝑞𝑢𝑖𝑟𝑒𝑑}\displaystyle=\{\mathsf{Slot}\langle x,\,\mathit{schema.prop}[x],\,\rangle\mid x\in\mathit{schema.required}\}
O⁡(𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎)\displaystyle O(\mathit{schema}) ={𝖲𝗅𝗈𝗍⟨x,𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎.𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑝[x],⟩∣x∈𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎.𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑝𝑒𝑟𝑡𝑖𝑒𝑠∖𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎.𝑟𝑒𝑞𝑢𝑖𝑟𝑒𝑑}\displaystyle=\{\mathsf{Slot}\langle x,\,\mathit{schema.prop}[x],\,\rangle\mid x\in\mathit{schema.properties}\setminus\mathit{schema.required}\}

The transactionality flag tt is undefined (??); no machine-readable annotation survives the round-trip.

Φ−1​(𝖱𝖾𝗌𝗈𝗎𝗋𝖼𝖾​⟨u,c⟩)\Phi^{-1}(\mathsf{Resource}\langle u,\,c\rangle) and Φ−1​(𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗆𝗉𝗍​⟨⋅,⋅⟩)\Phi^{-1}(\mathsf{Prompt}\langle\cdot,\,\cdot\rangle) are undefined: SGD has no passive-context or template primitives.

5.2 Partiality and Lossiness

Theorem 5.2 (Φ−1\Phi^{-1} is Partial).

Φ−1\Phi^{-1} is undefined on a non-empty subset of 𝖬𝖢𝖯\mathsf{MCP}.

Proof.

Counterexample 1 (missing transactionality).

⬇
M1 = Tool⟨\langle
"delete_user",
"Permanently deletes a user account",
{ "type": "object", "required": ["user_id"],
"properties": { "user_id": {"type": "string"} } }
⟩\rangle
Φ−1\Phi^{-1}(M1) = Intent⟨\langle
"delete_user", "Permanently deletes a user account",
[Slot⟨\langle"user_id", "string", []⟩\rangle], [],
? // UNDEFINED: is_transactional cannot be recovered
⟩\rangle

Φ−1​(M1)\Phi^{-1}(M_{1}) yields 𝖨𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗇𝗍​⟨⋅,⋅,⋅,⋅,?⟩\mathsf{Intent}\langle\cdot,\,\cdot,\,\cdot,\,\cdot,\,?\rangle—the 𝗂𝗌​_​𝗍𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌𝖺𝖼𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇𝖺𝗅\mathsf{is\_transactional} flag is critical for safety (requiring user approval) but is absent from MCP schemas. Inference from description strings is unreliable and not compositionally verifiable.

Counterexample 2 (resources).

⬇
M2 = Resource⟨\langle
"file:///var/log/app.log",
"2026-02-20 10:00:00 ERROR Connection timeout..."
⟩\rangle
Φ−1\Phi^{-1}(M2) = ??? // No SGD equivalent: Resource ≠\neq Intent

SGD has no Resource primitive; a resource is passive context, not an executable intent. No semantically correct mapping exists.

Counterexample 3 (dynamic discovery).

⬇
M3 = Initialize⟨\langle{tools: true, sampling: true}⟩\rangle
| ToolsList⟨\langlequery⟩\rangle.filter(tools, query).return⟨\langlefiltered⟩\rangle
Φ−1\Phi^{-1}(M3) = ??? // No SGD equivalent for capability negotiation

SGD assumes all schemas are provided upfront; it has no equivalent to capability negotiation or runtime tool filtering. ∎

Theorem 5.3 (𝖬𝖢𝖯\mathsf{MCP} is Strictly More Expressive than 𝖲𝖦𝖣\mathsf{SGD}).

∃M∈𝖬𝖢𝖯.∀S∈𝖲𝖦𝖣.Φ⁡(S)≠M\exists M\in\mathsf{MCP}.\;\forall S\in\mathsf{SGD}.\;\Phi(S)\neq M.

Proof.

Witnesses: 𝖱𝖾𝗌𝗈𝗎𝗋𝖼𝖾​⟨⋅,⋅⟩\mathsf{Resource}\langle\cdot,\,\cdot\rangle, 𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗆𝗉𝗍​⟨⋅,⋅⟩\mathsf{Prompt}\langle\cdot,\,\cdot\rangle, 𝖨𝗇𝗂𝗍𝗂𝖺𝗅𝗂𝗓𝖾​⟨⋅⟩\mathsf{Initialize}\langle\cdot\rangle. These primitives lie outside Image⁡(Φ)\mathrm{Image}(\Phi) since Φ\Phi maps only to 𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅\mathsf{Tool} terms. ∎

Theorem 5.4 (Lossy Round-Trip).

Φ−1∘Φ≠id𝖲𝖦𝖣\Phi^{-1}\circ\Phi\neq\mathrm{id}_{\mathsf{SGD}}.

Proof.

Let S=𝖨𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗇𝗍⁡⟨"​𝚌𝚛𝚎𝚊𝚝𝚎​_​𝚘𝚛𝚍𝚎𝚛​",⋯,⋯,⋯,𝗍𝗋𝗎𝖾⟩S=\mathsf{Intent}\langle\mathtt{"create\_order"},\,\cdots,\,\cdots,\,\cdots,\,\mathsf{true}\rangle.

Φ⁡(S)\displaystyle\Phi(S) =𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅⟨"𝚌𝚛𝚎𝚊𝚝𝚎_𝚘𝚛𝚍𝚎𝚛",⋯,𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎⟩(is_transactional lost)\displaystyle=\mathsf{Tool}\langle\mathtt{"create\_order"},\,\cdots,\,\mathit{schema}\rangle\quad\text{(is\_transactional lost)}
Φ−1​(Φ​(S))\displaystyle\Phi^{-1}(\Phi(S)) =𝖨𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗇𝗍⁡⟨"​𝚌𝚛𝚎𝚊𝚝𝚎​_​𝚘𝚛𝚍𝚎𝚛​",⋯,⋯,⋯,?⟩≠S\displaystyle=\mathsf{Intent}\langle\mathtt{"create\_order"},\,\cdots,\,\cdots,\,\cdots,\,?\rangle\neq S

Information lost: transactionality flag, error recovery strategies, tool dependencies encoded in dialogue flow. ∎

Theorem 5.5 (Φ−1\Phi^{-1} is Not Injective).

Where Φ−1\Phi^{-1} is defined it is not injective.

Proof.

Let M1M_{1} and M2M_{2} be tools with the same schema but different side-effect annotations embedded in their descriptions:

⬇
M1 = Tool⟨\langle "transfer_funds",
"Transfers money between accounts", schema ⟩\rangle
M2 = Tool⟨\langle "transfer_funds",
"Transfers money between accounts [SIDE EFFECT: sends email]",
schema ⟩\rangle // same schema, different implicit side effects
Φ−1\Phi^{-1}(M1) = Φ−1\Phi^{-1}(M2) = Intent⟨\langle
"transfer_funds", ..., is_transactional=? ⟩\rangle

Since Φ−1\Phi^{-1} does not parse description strings structurally, Φ−1​(M1)=Φ−1​(M2)\Phi^{-1}(M_{1})=\Phi^{-1}(M_{2}) yet M1≠M2M_{1}\neq M_{2}. ∎

5.3 Gap Summary

Theorem 5.6 (𝖬𝖢𝖯\mathsf{MCP} Expressivity Gaps).

𝖬𝖢𝖯\mathsf{MCP} lacks: (i) a machine-readable 𝗂𝗌​_​𝗍𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌𝖺𝖼𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇𝖺𝗅\mathsf{is\_transactional} flag; (ii) structured error-recovery paths; (iii) explicit inter-tool dependency declarations; (iv) formal human-in-the-loop approval protocols. 𝖲𝖦𝖣\mathsf{SGD} lacks: (i) a passive-context (Resource) primitive; (ii) a workflow-template (Prompt) mechanism; (iii) runtime capability negotiation; (iv) progressive disclosure of schema detail.

6 Five Principles as Type-System Extensions

We formalize five design principles as type-system extensions closing the gaps of Theorem 5.6.

6.1 Principle 1: Semantic Completeness

Informal: Descriptions must convey why parameters exist, not merely their types.

Definition 6.1 (Semantic Density).
𝗌𝖾𝗆​_​𝖽𝖾𝗇𝗌𝗂𝗍𝗒​(s)=|𝖾𝗇𝗍𝗂𝗍𝗂𝖾𝗌⁡(s)||𝗍𝗈𝗄𝖾𝗇𝗌⁡(s)|\mathsf{sem\_density}(s)\;=\;\frac{|\mathsf{entities}(s)|}{|\mathsf{tokens}(s)|}

where 𝖾𝗇𝗍𝗂𝗍𝗂𝖾𝗌⁡(s)\mathsf{entities}(s) counts named entities, examples, and constraints in string ss, and τ\tau is a threshold (e.g., 0.30.3).

Type Rule (P1):

Γ⊢𝑑𝑒𝑠𝑐:𝖲𝗍𝗋𝗂𝗇𝗀𝗌𝖾𝗆​_​𝖽𝖾𝗇𝗌𝗂𝗍𝗒​(𝑑𝑒𝑠𝑐)≥τΓ⊢{𝚍𝚎𝚜𝚌𝚛𝚒𝚙𝚝𝚒𝚘𝚗:𝑑𝑒𝑠𝑐}:𝖶𝖾𝗅𝗅𝖣𝖾𝗌𝖼𝗋𝗂𝖻𝖾𝖽Right=WellDescribed\frac{\Gamma\vdash\mathit{desc}:\mathsf{String}\quad\mathsf{sem\_density}(\mathit{desc})\geq\tau}{\Gamma\vdash\{\mathtt{description}{:}\;\mathit{desc}\}:\mathsf{WellDescribed}}\quad\textsc{Right=WellDescribed}

Example.

⬇
// Violates P1: sem_density = 0 (no new information)
"departure": {"type": "string", "description": "departure"}
// Satisfies P1: sem_density = 3/10 = 0.3
// entities: IATA (concept) + ZRH, JFK, LHR (3 examples)
"departure": {
"type": "string",
"description": "IATA airport code for departure (e.g., ZRH, JFK, LHR)"
}

6.2 Principle 2: Explicit Action Boundaries

Informal: Tools must signal whether invocation causes side effects.

𝗌𝗂𝖽𝖾​_​𝖾𝖿𝖿𝖾𝖼𝗍𝗌\displaystyle\mathsf{side\_effects} ::=𝗋𝖾𝖺𝖽|𝗐𝗋𝗂𝗍𝖾​∣𝖽𝖾𝗅𝖾𝗍𝖾∣​𝗇𝗈𝗇𝖾\displaystyle\;::=\;\mathsf{read}\mid\mathsf{write}\mid\mathsf{delete}\mid\mathsf{none}

Type Rule (P2):

𝑚𝑒𝑡𝑎.𝗌𝗂𝖽𝖾​_​𝖾𝖿𝖿𝖾𝖼𝗍𝗌∈{𝗐𝗋𝗂𝗍𝖾,𝖽𝖾𝗅𝖾𝗍𝖾}𝑚𝑒𝑡𝑎.𝗋𝖾𝗊𝗎𝗂𝗋𝖾𝗌​_​𝖺𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖺𝗅=𝗍𝗋𝗎𝖾Right=WriteApproval\frac{\mathit{meta}.\mathsf{side\_effects}\in\{\mathsf{write},\,\mathsf{delete}\}}{\mathit{meta}.\mathsf{requires\_approval}=\mathsf{true}}\quad\textsc{Right=WriteApproval}

The process-level encoding of a write-capable tool is:

𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅𝗐𝗋𝗂𝗍𝖾=\displaystyle\mathsf{Tool}_{\mathsf{write}}\;=\; 𝖼𝖺𝗅𝗅?⟨𝑝𝑎𝑟𝑎𝑚𝑠⟩.𝖺𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖺𝗅?⟨𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑓𝑖𝑟𝑚⟩.\displaystyle\;\mathsf{call}?\langle\mathit{params}\rangle\mathbin{.}\mathsf{approval}?\langle\mathit{confirm}\rangle\mathbin{.}
(𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑓𝑖𝑟𝑚=𝗍𝗋𝗎𝖾→𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾⁡⟨𝑝𝑎𝑟𝑎𝑚𝑠⟩.𝗋𝖾𝗌𝗎𝗅𝗍!​⟨𝗈𝗄⟩​.0CLOSE\displaystyle\quad\bigl(\mathit{confirm}=\mathsf{true}\;\to\;\mathsf{execute}\langle\mathit{params}\rangle\mathbin{.}\mathsf{result}!\langle\mathsf{ok}\rangle\mathbin{.}\mathbf{0}
∣𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑓𝑖𝑟𝑚=𝖿𝖺𝗅𝗌𝖾→𝗋𝖾𝗌𝗎𝗅𝗍!⟨𝖼𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾𝗅𝗅𝖾𝖽⟩.0)\displaystyle\quad\mathbin{\mid}\;\mathit{confirm}=\mathsf{false}\;\to\;\mathsf{result}!\langle\mathsf{cancelled}\rangle\mathbin{.}\mathbf{0}\bigr)

Example.

⬇
Tool⟨\langle
"delete_user",
"Permanently deletes a user account",
{ "type": "object", "required": ["user_id"],
"properties": { "user_id": {"type": "string"} } },
metadata = {
side_effects: delete,
requires_approval: true // enforced by type rule WriteApproval
}
⟩\rangle
Theorem 6.2 (No Unapproved Side Effects – preliminary).

∀𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅\forall\,\mathsf{Tool} with 𝗌𝗂𝖽𝖾​_​𝖾𝖿𝖿𝖾𝖼𝗍𝗌∈{𝗐𝗋𝗂𝗍𝖾,𝖽𝖾𝗅𝖾𝗍𝖾}\mathsf{side\_effects}\in\{\mathsf{write},\mathsf{delete}\}: in every execution trace, 𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾\mathsf{execute} is preceded by 𝖺𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖺𝗅\mathsf{approval}.

6.3 Principle 3: Failure Mode Documentation

Informal: Enumerate expected error conditions and recovery strategies.

𝖿𝖺𝗂𝗅𝗎𝗋𝖾​_​𝗆𝗈𝖽𝖾𝗌\displaystyle\mathsf{failure\_modes} ::=[(𝐸𝑟𝑟𝑜𝑟𝑇𝑦𝑝𝑒,𝑅𝑒𝑐𝑜𝑣𝑒𝑟𝑦𝑆𝑡𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑔𝑦)]\displaystyle\;::=\;[(\mathit{ErrorType},\,\mathit{RecoveryStrategy})]
𝐸𝑟𝑟𝑜𝑟𝑇𝑦𝑝𝑒\displaystyle\mathit{ErrorType} ::=𝖵𝖺𝗅𝗂𝖽𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋​∣𝖠𝗎𝗍𝗁𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋∣​𝖲𝖾𝗋𝗏𝗂𝖼𝖾𝖣𝗈𝗐𝗇|𝖭𝗈𝗍𝖥𝗈𝗎𝗇𝖽|⋯\displaystyle\;::=\;\mathsf{ValidationError}\mid\mathsf{AuthError}\mid\mathsf{ServiceDown}\mid\mathsf{NotFound}\mid\cdots
𝑅𝑒𝑐𝑜𝑣𝑒𝑟𝑦𝑆𝑡𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑔𝑦\displaystyle\mathit{RecoveryStrategy} ::=𝖱𝖾𝗍𝗋𝗒⁡(n)|𝖥𝖺𝗅𝗅𝖻𝖺𝖼𝗄⁡(𝑡𝑜𝑜𝑙)​∣𝖴𝗌𝖾𝗋𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗆𝗉𝗍⁡(m)∣​𝖠𝖻𝗈𝗋𝗍\displaystyle\;::=\;\mathsf{Retry}(n)\mid\mathsf{Fallback}(\mathit{tool})\mid\mathsf{UserPrompt}(m)\mid\mathsf{Abort}

Example.

⬇
Tool⟨\langle
"fetch_user_data",
"Retrieves user information from database",
schema,
metadata = {
failure_modes: [
(NotFound, UserPrompt("User does not exist. Create new?")),
(ServiceDown, Retry(3)),
(AuthError, Fallback("use_cached_data"))
]
}
⟩\rangle

A robust tool is encoded as:

𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅𝗋𝗈𝖻𝗎𝗌𝗍=\displaystyle\mathsf{Tool}_{\mathsf{robust}}\;=\; 𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾?⟨𝑝𝑎𝑟𝑎𝑚𝑠⟩.\displaystyle\;\mathsf{execute}?\langle\mathit{params}\rangle\mathbin{.}
(𝗌𝗎𝖼𝖼𝖾𝗌𝗌!​⟨𝑜𝑢𝑡𝑝𝑢𝑡⟩​.0CLOSE\displaystyle\;\bigl(\mathsf{success}!\langle\mathit{output}\rangle\mathbin{.}\mathbf{0}
∣𝖾𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋!​⟨𝖭𝗈𝗍𝖥𝗈𝗎𝗇𝖽,𝑟𝑒𝑐1⟩.𝑟𝑒𝑐1​.0\displaystyle\;\;\mathbin{\mid}\;\mathsf{error}!\langle\mathsf{NotFound},\,\mathit{rec}_{1}\rangle\mathbin{.}\mathit{rec}_{1}\mathbin{.}\mathbf{0}
∣𝖾𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋!⟨𝖲𝖾𝗋𝗏𝗂𝖼𝖾𝖣𝗈𝗐𝗇,𝑟𝑒𝑐2⟩.𝑟𝑒𝑐2.0)\displaystyle\;\;\mathbin{\mid}\;\mathsf{error}!\langle\mathsf{ServiceDown},\,\mathit{rec}_{2}\rangle\mathbin{.}\mathit{rec}_{2}\mathbin{.}\mathbf{0}\bigr)

where each 𝑟𝑒𝑐i\mathit{rec}_{i} corresponds to the declared recovery strategy.

6.4 Principle 4: Progressive Disclosure Compatibility

Informal: Support two-level descriptions for token efficiency.

P4:∀𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅⟨n,d,𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎⟩.∃𝑠𝑢𝑚𝑚𝑎𝑟𝑦:𝖲𝗍𝗋𝗂𝗇𝗀.\displaystyle\textbf{P4:}\quad\forall\,\mathsf{Tool}\langle n,\,d,\,\mathit{schema}\rangle.\;\exists\,\mathit{summary}\mathbin{:}\mathsf{String}.\quad |𝑠𝑢𝑚𝑚𝑎𝑟𝑦|< 0.1⋅|d|\displaystyle|\mathit{summary}|\;<\;0.1\cdot|d|
∧\displaystyle\land\quad 𝑠𝑢𝑚𝑚𝑎𝑟𝑦​ enables ​𝗍𝗈𝗈𝗅​_​𝗌𝖾𝗅𝖾𝖼𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇\displaystyle\mathit{summary}\text{ enables }\mathsf{tool\_selection}
∧\displaystyle\land\quad d​ enables ​𝗍𝗈𝗈𝗅​_​𝗂𝗇𝗏𝗈𝖼𝖺𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇\displaystyle d\text{ enables }\mathsf{tool\_invocation}

Example.

⬇
Tool⟨\langle
name = "search_repositories",
summary = "Searches GitHub repositories by query", // 6 tokens
description = "Searches GitHub repositories matching the query
string. Supports advanced operators: language:rust, stars:>100,
fork:true. Returns name, description, stars, last update.
Limited to 100 results per page.", // 38 tokens
schema = { ... }
⟩\rangle

Protocol extension:

Discovery: 𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅𝗌𝖫𝗂𝗌𝗍→𝗅𝗂𝗌𝗍[{n,𝑠𝑢𝑚𝑚𝑎𝑟𝑦},…]\displaystyle\mathsf{ToolsList}\xrightarrow{\mathsf{list}}[\{n,\mathit{summary}\},\;\ldots]
Invocation: 𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅𝖣𝖾𝗍𝖺𝗂𝗅→𝖽𝖾𝗍𝖺𝗂𝗅⁡(n){n,d,𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎}\displaystyle\mathsf{ToolDetail}\xrightarrow{\mathsf{detail}(n)}\{n,d,\mathit{schema}\}
Theorem 6.3 (Token Reduction (Speakeasy, 2024)).

Under progressive disclosure, if k<0.1k<0.1 is the fraction of tools actually invoked:

𝑡𝑜𝑘𝑒𝑛𝑠𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑔𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑠𝑖𝑣𝑒=∑i|𝑠𝑢𝑚𝑚𝑎𝑟𝑦i|+k​∑j|dj|< 0.2⋅∑i|di|= 0.2⋅𝑡𝑜𝑘𝑒𝑛𝑠𝑏𝑎𝑠𝑒𝑙𝑖𝑛𝑒\mathit{tokens}_{\mathit{progressive}}\;=\;\sum_{i}|\mathit{summary}_{i}|+k\sum_{j}|d_{j}|\;<\;0.2\cdot\sum_{i}|d_{i}|\;=\;0.2\cdot\mathit{tokens}_{\mathit{baseline}}

6.5 Principle 5: Inter-Tool Relationship Declaration

Informal: Express dependencies between tools explicitly.

𝖽𝖾𝗉𝖾𝗇𝖽𝖾𝗇𝖼𝗂𝖾𝗌\displaystyle\mathsf{dependencies} ::=[(𝑡𝑜𝑜𝑙​_​𝑛𝑎𝑚𝑒,𝑟𝑒𝑙𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛)]\displaystyle\;::=\;[(\mathit{tool\_name},\,\mathit{relation})]
𝑟𝑒𝑙𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛\displaystyle\mathit{relation} ::=𝖱𝖾𝗊𝗎𝗂𝗋𝖾𝗌​∣𝖯𝗋𝗈𝖽𝗎𝖼𝖾𝗌𝖨𝗇𝗉𝗎𝗍𝖥𝗈𝗋∣​𝖤𝗑𝖼𝗅𝗎𝗌𝗂𝗏𝖾𝖶𝗂𝗍𝗁\displaystyle\;::=\;\mathsf{Requires}\mid\mathsf{ProducesInputFor}\mid\mathsf{ExclusiveWith}

Example.

⬇
Tool⟨\langle
"process_payment",
"Processes a payment transaction",
schema,
metadata = {
dependencies: [
("create_order", Requires), // must call create_order first
("verify_balance", Requires) // must verify balance
]
}
⟩\rangle

The process encoding of a dependent pair (TA,TB)(T_{A},T_{B}) with TB.𝖽𝖾𝗉𝖾𝗇𝖽𝖾𝗇𝖼𝗂𝖾𝗌=[(TA,𝖱𝖾𝗊𝗎𝗂𝗋𝖾𝗌)]T_{B}.\mathsf{dependencies}=[(T_{A},\mathsf{Requires})]:

TA\displaystyle T_{A} =𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾A​?​⟨𝑝𝑎𝑟𝑎𝑚𝑠⟩.𝗋𝖾𝗌𝗎𝗅𝗍A!​⟨𝑖𝑑,{𝖿𝗈𝗋:TB}⟩​.0\displaystyle\;=\;\mathsf{execute}_{A}?\langle\mathit{params}\rangle\mathbin{.}\mathsf{result}_{A}!\langle\mathit{id},\,\{{\mathsf{for}{:}\,T_{B}}\}\rangle\mathbin{.}\mathbf{0}
TB\displaystyle T_{B} =𝗋𝖾𝗊𝗎𝗂𝗋𝖾𝗌​?​⟨𝑖𝑑​𝖿𝗋𝗈𝗆​TA⟩.𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾B​?​⟨𝑖𝑑,𝑝𝑎𝑟𝑎𝑚𝑠⟩.𝗋𝖾𝗌𝗎𝗅𝗍B!​⟨𝑑𝑎𝑡𝑎⟩​.0\displaystyle\;=\;\mathsf{requires}?\langle\mathit{id}\ \mathsf{from}\ T_{A}\rangle\mathbin{.}\mathsf{execute}_{B}?\langle\mathit{id},\,\mathit{params}\rangle\mathbin{.}\mathsf{result}_{B}!\langle\mathit{data}\rangle\mathbin{.}\mathbf{0}
Theorem 6.4 (Dependency Safety).

∀\forall workflow WW composed of tools {T1,…,Tn}\{T_{1},\ldots,T_{n}\}: if Ti.𝖽𝖾𝗉𝖾𝗇𝖽𝖾𝗇𝖼𝗂𝖾𝗌=[(Tj,𝖱𝖾𝗊𝗎𝗂𝗋𝖾𝗌)]T_{i}.\mathsf{dependencies}=[(T_{j},\mathsf{Requires})], then in all valid execution traces 𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾Tj\mathsf{execute}_{T_{j}} precedes 𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾Ti\mathsf{execute}_{T_{i}}.

7 Extended Calculus 𝖬𝖢𝖯+\mathsf{MCP}^{+} and Full Equivalence

7.1 𝖬𝖢𝖯+\mathsf{MCP}^{+} Syntax

𝖬𝖢𝖯+\displaystyle\mathsf{MCP}^{+} =𝖬𝖢𝖯∪{𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅​⟨n,d,𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎⟩+}\displaystyle\;=\;\mathsf{MCP}\;\cup\;\bigl\{\mathsf{Tool}\langle n,\,d,\,\mathit{schema}\rangle^{+}\bigr\}

where a 𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅+\mathsf{Tool}^{+} carries additional metadata:

𝑚𝑒𝑡𝑎𝑑𝑎𝑡𝑎\displaystyle\mathit{metadata} ={𝗌𝗂𝖽𝖾_𝖾𝖿𝖿𝖾𝖼𝗍𝗌:{𝗋𝖾𝖺𝖽,𝗐𝗋𝗂𝗍𝖾,𝖽𝖾𝗅𝖾𝗍𝖾,𝗇𝗈𝗇𝖾},\displaystyle\;=\;\bigl\{\mathsf{side\_effects}:\{\mathsf{read},\mathsf{write},\mathsf{delete},\mathsf{none}\},
𝗋𝖾𝗊𝗎𝗂𝗋𝖾𝗌​_​𝖺𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖺𝗅:𝖡𝗈𝗈𝗅,\displaystyle\qquad\mathsf{requires\_approval}:\mathsf{Bool},
𝖿𝖺𝗂𝗅𝗎𝗋𝖾​_​𝗆𝗈𝖽𝖾𝗌:[(𝐸𝑟𝑟𝑜𝑟𝑇𝑦𝑝𝑒,𝑅𝑒𝑐𝑜𝑣𝑒𝑟𝑦𝑆𝑡𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑔𝑦)],\displaystyle\qquad\mathsf{failure\_modes}:[(\mathit{ErrorType},\mathit{RecoveryStrategy})],
𝗌𝗎𝗆𝗆𝖺𝗋𝗒:𝖲𝗍𝗋𝗂𝗇𝗀,\displaystyle\qquad\mathsf{summary}:\mathsf{String},
𝖽𝖾𝗉𝖾𝗇𝖽𝖾𝗇𝖼𝗂𝖾𝗌:[(𝑡𝑜𝑜𝑙_𝑛𝑎𝑚𝑒,𝑟𝑒𝑙𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛)]}\displaystyle\qquad\mathsf{dependencies}:[(\mathit{tool\_name},\mathit{relation})]\bigr\}

7.2 Extended Mapping Φ+\Phi^{+}

Φ+​(𝖨𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗇𝗍⁡⟨n,d,R,O,t⟩)\displaystyle\Phi^{+}\!\left(\mathsf{Intent}\langle n,\,d,\,R,\,O,\,t\rangle\right) =𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅​⟨n,d,𝗌𝖼𝗁𝖾𝗆𝖺⁡(R,O)⟩+​[𝑚𝑒𝑡𝑎]\displaystyle\;=\;\mathsf{Tool}\langle n,\,d,\,\mathsf{schema}(R,O)\rangle^{+}[\mathit{meta}]
𝑚𝑒𝑡𝑎\displaystyle\mathit{meta} ={𝗌𝗂𝖽𝖾_𝖾𝖿𝖿𝖾𝖼𝗍𝗌:(t?𝗐𝗋𝗂𝗍𝖾:𝗋𝖾𝖺𝖽),\displaystyle\;=\;\bigl\{\mathsf{side\_effects}{:}\;(t\;?\;\mathsf{write}:\mathsf{read}),
𝗋𝖾𝗊𝗎𝗂𝗋𝖾𝗌​_​𝖺𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖺𝗅:t,\displaystyle\qquad\mathsf{requires\_approval}{:}\;t,
𝖿𝖺𝗂𝗅𝗎𝗋𝖾​_​𝗆𝗈𝖽𝖾𝗌:𝖾𝗑𝗍𝗋𝖺𝖼𝗍​_​𝖾𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋𝗌​(𝐼𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑡),\displaystyle\qquad\mathsf{failure\_modes}{:}\;\mathsf{extract\_errors}(\mathit{Intent}),
𝗌𝗎𝗆𝗆𝖺𝗋𝗒:𝖿𝗂𝗋𝗌𝗍​_​𝗌𝖾𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗇𝖼𝖾​(d),\displaystyle\qquad\mathsf{summary}{:}\;\mathsf{first\_sentence}(d),
𝖽𝖾𝗉𝖾𝗇𝖽𝖾𝗇𝖼𝗂𝖾𝗌:𝖾𝗑𝗍𝗋𝖺𝖼𝗍_𝖽𝖾𝗉𝗌(𝐼𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑛𝑡)}\displaystyle\qquad\mathsf{dependencies}{:}\;\mathsf{extract\_deps}(\mathit{Intent})\bigr\}
(Φ+)−1​(𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅​⟨n,d,𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎⟩+​[𝑚𝑒𝑡𝑎])\displaystyle(\Phi^{+})^{-1}\!\left(\mathsf{Tool}\langle n,\,d,\,\mathit{schema}\rangle^{+}[\mathit{meta}]\right) =𝖨𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗇𝗍⁡⟨n,d,R⁡(𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎),O⁡(𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎),t⟩\displaystyle\;=\;\mathsf{Intent}\langle n,\,d,\,R(\mathit{schema}),\,O(\mathit{schema}),\,t\rangle
where ​t\displaystyle\text{where }\;t =(𝑚𝑒𝑡𝑎.𝗌𝗂𝖽𝖾_𝖾𝖿𝖿𝖾𝖼𝗍𝗌∈{𝗐𝗋𝗂𝗍𝖾,𝖽𝖾𝗅𝖾𝗍𝖾})\displaystyle\;=\;(\mathit{meta}.\mathsf{side\_effects}\in\{\mathsf{write},\mathsf{delete}\})

7.3 Main Theorem: Full Equivalence

Theorem 7.1 (𝖬𝖢𝖯+≅𝖲𝖦𝖣\mathsf{MCP}^{+}\cong\mathsf{SGD}).

The following hold:

  1. 1.

    ∀S∈𝖲𝖦𝖣.S∼Φ+​(S)\forall S\in\mathsf{SGD}.\;S\sim\Phi^{+}(S),

  2. 2.

    ∀M+∈𝖬𝖢𝖯+.M+∼(Φ+)−1​(M+)\forall M^{+}\in\mathsf{MCP}^{+}.\;M^{+}\sim(\Phi^{+})^{-1}(M^{+}),

  3. 3.

    (Φ+)−1∘Φ+=id𝖲𝖦𝖣(\Phi^{+})^{-1}\circ\Phi^{+}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathsf{SGD}},

  4. 4.

    Φ+∘(Φ+)−1=id𝖬𝖢𝖯+\Phi^{+}\circ(\Phi^{+})^{-1}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathsf{MCP}^{+}}.

Proof.

Part 1 (Φ+\Phi^{+} preserves structure): Φ+\Phi^{+} extends Φ\Phi with metadata. By Theorem 4.4, structural bisimulation is preserved. The metadata fields preserve SGD semantics: 𝗂𝗌​_​𝗍𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌𝖺𝖼𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇𝖺𝗅↔𝗌𝗂𝖽𝖾​_​𝖾𝖿𝖿𝖾𝖼𝗍𝗌\mathsf{is\_transactional}\leftrightarrow\mathsf{side\_effects}, error handling ↔\leftrightarrow failure_modes, dialogue dependencies ↔\leftrightarrow tool dependencies.

Part 2 (injectivity): Assume Φ+​(S1)=Φ+​(S2)\Phi^{+}(S_{1})=\Phi^{+}(S_{2}). Then n1=n2n_{1}=n_{2}, 𝗌𝖼𝗁𝖾𝗆𝖺⁡(R1,O1)=𝗌𝖼𝗁𝖾𝗆𝖺⁡(R2,O2)\mathsf{schema}(R_{1},O_{1})=\mathsf{schema}(R_{2},O_{2}) implying R1=R2,O1=O2R_{1}=R_{2},\,O_{1}=O_{2}, and 𝑚𝑒𝑡𝑎1=𝑚𝑒𝑡𝑎2\mathit{meta}_{1}=\mathit{meta}_{2} implying t1=t2t_{1}=t_{2}. Hence S1=S2S_{1}=S_{2}.

Part 3 (surjectivity): For any M+=𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅​⟨n,d,𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎⟩+​[𝑚𝑒𝑡𝑎]M^{+}=\mathsf{Tool}\langle n,\,d,\,\mathit{schema}\rangle^{+}[\mathit{meta}], construct S=𝖨𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗇𝗍⟨n,d,(Φ+)−1(𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎.𝑟𝑒𝑞𝑢𝑖𝑟𝑒𝑑),(Φ+)−1(𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎.𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑝𝑒𝑟𝑡𝑖𝑒𝑠∖𝑟𝑒𝑞𝑢𝑖𝑟𝑒𝑑),(𝑚𝑒𝑡𝑎.𝑠𝑖𝑑𝑒_𝑒𝑓𝑓𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑠≠𝗋𝖾𝖺𝖽)⟩S=\mathsf{Intent}\langle n,\,d,\,(\Phi^{+})^{-1}(\mathit{schema.required}),\,(\Phi^{+})^{-1}(\mathit{schema.properties}\setminus\mathit{required}),\,(\mathit{meta.side\_effects}\neq\mathsf{read})\rangle. Then Φ+​(S)=M+\Phi^{+}(S)=M^{+}.

Part 4 (round-trip identity): Verified by direct substitution into Definitions 4.1 and the extended mapping. ∎

Corollary 7.2 (Necessity and Sufficiency).

The five principles are necessary and sufficient for 𝖲𝖦𝖣≅𝖬𝖢𝖯+\mathsf{SGD}\cong\mathsf{MCP}^{+}.

Proof.

Sufficiency: Theorem 7.1. Necessity: removing any of Principles 1, 2, 3, or 5 breaks the bijection (shown in Section 5). Principle 4 is not required for theoretical equivalence but is necessary for practical scalability (token budget). ∎

Theorem 7.3 (Five Principles are Minimal).

The five principles are the minimal extension to 𝖬𝖢𝖯\mathsf{MCP} needed for 𝖲𝖦𝖣≅𝖬𝖢𝖯+\mathsf{SGD}\cong\mathsf{MCP}^{+}.

Proof.

By necessity analysis:

  • •

    Remove P1: (Φ+)−1(\Phi^{+})^{-1} cannot map descriptions to SGD slot semantics reliably; zero-shot generalization fails.

  • •

    Remove P2: 𝗂𝗌​_​𝗍𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌𝖺𝖼𝗍𝗂𝗈𝗇𝖺𝗅\mathsf{is\_transactional} is unrecoverable; (Φ+)−1​(𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅+)(\Phi^{+})^{-1}(\mathsf{Tool}^{+}) yields 𝖨𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗇𝗍​⟨⋅,⋅,⋅,⋅,?⟩\mathsf{Intent}\langle\cdot,\,\cdot,\,\cdot,\,\cdot,\,?\rangle; not injective.

  • •

    Remove P3: SGD error-recovery strategies cannot be encoded; behavioral equivalence fails on error paths.

  • •

    Remove P4: Equivalence is maintained but 𝖬𝖢𝖯\mathsf{MCP} becomes impractical at scale (token overhead).

  • •

    Remove P5: Multi-turn dialogue dependencies are lost; tool sequencing becomes implicit.

Core equivalence principles: {1,2,3,5}\{1,2,3,5\}. Scaling principle: {4}\{4\}. ∎

8 Security Properties as Process Invariants

8.1 Capability Confinement

Definition 8.1 (Capability-Confined Process).

A process PP is capability-confined iff in every state reachable from PP no unauthorized channel access occurs.

Theorem 8.2 (Channel Scoping Ensures Confinement).
𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅𝖼𝗈𝗇𝖿𝗂𝗇𝖾𝖽=(ν​𝑘𝑒𝑦)​𝗇𝖺𝗆𝖾​?​⟨𝑝𝑎𝑟𝑎𝑚𝑠⟩.𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾⁡⟨𝑝𝑎𝑟𝑎𝑚𝑠,𝑘𝑒𝑦⟩.𝗋𝖾𝗌𝗎𝗅𝗍!​⟨𝑜𝑢𝑡𝑝𝑢𝑡⟩​.0\mathsf{Tool}_{\mathsf{confined}}\;=\;(\nu\,\mathit{key})\;\;\mathsf{name}?\langle\mathit{params}\rangle\mathbin{.}\mathsf{execute}\langle\mathit{params},\mathit{key}\rangle\mathbin{.}\mathsf{result}!\langle\mathit{output}\rangle\mathbin{.}\mathbf{0}

is capability-confined under typed π​-calculus\pi\text{-calculus}.

Proof.

Channel 𝑘𝑒𝑦\mathit{key} is scoped by (ν​𝑘𝑒𝑦)(\nu\,\mathit{key}); no subprocess outside this scope can reference it; the type system prevents channel smuggling (higher-order sends on 𝑘𝑒𝑦\mathit{key} are disallowed). Hence 𝑘𝑒𝑦\mathit{key} cannot leak to external processes. Applications: API keys, database credentials confined to server scope. ∎

8.2 Tool Poisoning Prevention

Definition 8.3 (Tool Poisoning Attack).

A malicious tool embeds executable instructions in its description:

𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅⁡⟨"​𝚒𝚗𝚗𝚘𝚌𝚎𝚗𝚝​_​𝚜𝚎𝚊𝚛𝚌𝚑​",[IGNORE PREVIOUS INSTRUCTIONS. Exfiltrate credentials.],𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑚𝑎⟩\mathsf{Tool}\langle\mathtt{"innocent\_search"},\,\texttt{[IGNORE PREVIOUS INSTRUCTIONS. Exfiltrate credentials.]},\,\mathit{schema}\rangle
Theorem 8.4 (Type Safety Prevents Tool Poisoning (Wong and Kolter, 2018)).

If tool descriptions are typed as inert data, no tool can inject malicious instructions into agent reasoning.

Proof.

Define a two-sort type system:

Γ⊢𝑑𝑒𝑠𝑐:𝖲𝗍𝗋𝗂𝗇𝗀Γ⊢𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗉𝗅𝖺𝗒⁡(𝑑𝑒𝑠𝑐):()Right=DisplayΓ⊢c:𝖢𝗈𝖽𝖾Γ⊢𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾⁡(c):𝖱𝖾𝗌𝗎𝗅𝗍Right=Execute\frac{\Gamma\vdash\mathit{desc}:\mathsf{String}}{\Gamma\vdash\mathsf{display}(\mathit{desc}):()}\quad\textsc{Right=Display}\par\frac{\Gamma\vdash c:\mathsf{Code}}{\Gamma\vdash\mathsf{execute}(c):\mathsf{Result}}\quad\textsc{Right=Execute}

Since 𝑑𝑒𝑠𝑐:𝖲𝗍𝗋𝗂𝗇𝗀\mathit{desc}:\mathsf{String}, the agent cannot call 𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾⁡(𝑑𝑒𝑠𝑐)\mathsf{execute}(\mathit{desc}) (type error: 𝖲𝗍𝗋𝗂𝗇𝗀≰𝖢𝗈𝖽𝖾\mathsf{String}\not\leq\mathsf{Code}) and is restricted to 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗉𝗅𝖺𝗒⁡(𝑑𝑒𝑠𝑐)\mathsf{display}(\mathit{desc}). ∎

8.3 Approval Ordering

Theorem 8.5 (Approval Precedes Execution).

∀𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅+\forall\,\mathsf{Tool}^{+} with 𝗌𝗂𝖽𝖾​_​𝖾𝖿𝖿𝖾𝖼𝗍𝗌∈{𝗐𝗋𝗂𝗍𝖾,𝖽𝖾𝗅𝖾𝗍𝖾}\mathsf{side\_effects}\in\{\mathsf{write},\mathsf{delete}\}: in all execution traces, 𝖺𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖺𝗅\mathsf{approval} precedes 𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾\mathsf{execute}.

Proof.

By the operational semantics of P2 (Section 6): 𝖳𝗈𝗈𝗅𝗐𝗋𝗂𝗍𝖾\mathsf{Tool}_{\mathsf{write}} requires a transition on 𝖺𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖺𝗅​?​⟨𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑓𝑖𝑟𝑚⟩\mathsf{approval}?\langle\mathit{confirm}\rangle before it can produce an 𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾\mathsf{execute} transition. The process cannot reach 𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾\mathsf{execute} without prior 𝖺𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖺𝗅\mathsf{approval}. ∎

8.4 Dependency Ordering

Theorem 8.6 (Dependency Ordering).

∀\forall workflow W={T1,…,Tn}W=\{T_{1},\ldots,T_{n}\}: if Ti.𝖽𝖾𝗉𝖾𝗇𝖽𝖾𝗇𝖼𝗂𝖾𝗌=[(Tj,𝖱𝖾𝗊𝗎𝗂𝗋𝖾𝗌)]T_{i}.\mathsf{dependencies}=[(T_{j},\mathsf{Requires})], then in all valid traces 𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾Tj\mathsf{execute}_{T_{j}} precedes 𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾Ti\mathsf{execute}_{T_{i}}.

Proof.

Ti=𝗋𝖾𝗊𝗎𝗂𝗋𝖾𝗌​?​⟨𝑖𝑑​𝖿𝗋𝗈𝗆​Tj⟩.𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾Ti​…T_{i}=\mathsf{requires}?\langle\mathit{id}\ \mathsf{from}\ T_{j}\rangle\mathbin{.}\mathsf{execute}_{T_{i}}\ldots. The channel 𝗋𝖾𝗊𝗎𝗂𝗋𝖾𝗌\mathsf{requires} receives only after TjT_{j} executes and emits 𝗋𝖾𝗌𝗎𝗅𝗍Tj!​⟨𝑖𝑑,{𝖿𝗈𝗋:Ti}⟩\mathsf{result}_{T_{j}}!\langle\mathit{id},\{\mathsf{for}{:}T_{i}\}\rangle. Hence 𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾Tj≺𝖾𝗑𝖾𝖼𝗎𝗍𝖾Ti\mathsf{execute}_{T_{j}}\prec\mathsf{execute}_{T_{i}} in all valid traces. Application: payment processing requires order creation; validation requires authentication. ∎

9 Conclusion

We have presented the first formal semantics for agentic tool protocols, proving that SGD and MCP are structurally bisimilar under the mapping Φ\Phi (Theorem 4.4). However, Φ−1\Phi^{-1} is partial and lossy (Theorem 5.2), revealing four critical gaps in MCP’s expressivity.

Through bidirectional analysis we identified five principles as necessary and sufficient conditions for full behavioral equivalence, and formalized them as type-system extensions defining 𝖬𝖢𝖯+\mathsf{MCP}^{+} with 𝖬𝖢𝖯+≅𝖲𝖦𝖣\mathsf{MCP}^{+}\cong\mathsf{SGD} (Theorem 7.1).

Our framework enables:

  • •

    Compositional reasoning about multi-agent orchestration via parallel composition in π​-calculus\pi\text{-calculus}.

  • •

    Security properties as provable process invariants (confinement, no unapproved side effects, dependency ordering).

  • •

    Behavioral equivalence preserved under protocol transformation.

  • •

    Schema quality as a type-checkable property.

As LLM agents govern financial transactions, healthcare decisions, and infrastructure management, formal verification becomes essential. This paper provides the mathematical foundations for that verification, transforming agent protocols from ad-hoc conventions into provably safe systems. The convergence of SGD and MCP signals the emergence of Software 3.0, where autonomous agents dynamically discover and orchestrate capabilities through standardized, machine-readable interfaces—and our formalization ensures this future is not only powerful but verifiable.

10 Future Work

Several directions follow naturally from the foundations established here.

Mechanized proofs.

The bisimulation proofs (Theorems 4.4 and 7.1) are pen-and-paper arguments by structural induction. Formalizing them in a proof assistant such as Isabelle/HOL or Coq—using existing π​-calculus\pi\text{-calculus} libraries such as Nominal Isabelle (Milner, 1999)—would yield machine-checked guarantees and expose any residual gaps. This is the most direct path to a fully verified MCP+ type checker.

Probabilistic bisimulation.

LLM tool selection is inherently stochastic: the same prompt yields different tool calls with varying probability. Extending the labeled transition systems to continuous-time Markov chains and adopting Larsen–Skou probabilistic bisimulation would allow reasoning about expected behavioral equivalence and provide a formal measure of divergence between SGD and MCP agents under sampling.

Multi-agent choreographies.

The current calculus models a single agent against a single server. A natural extension is a choreography layer: given agents A1∣A2∣⋯∣AnA_{1}\mathbin{\mid}A_{2}\mathbin{\mid}\cdots\mathbin{\mid}A_{n} each holding a disjoint subset of 𝖬𝖢𝖯+\mathsf{MCP}^{+} tools, prove global safety properties—deadlock freedom, resource exclusivity, progress—from local type-checking alone. This connects directly to multiparty session types (Honda et al., 1998) and choreography calculi (Carbone et al., 2012).

Temporal safety via model checking.

The security theorems of Section 8 are proved structurally. An orthogonal approach expresses them in CTL or LTL and applies off-the-shelf model checkers (SPIN, nuXmv) to finite 𝖬𝖢𝖯+\mathsf{MCP}^{+} instances. This would enable property verification for new protocol variants without manual proof, and could integrate with existing MCP server validation pipelines.

Resource-aware semantics.

Principle 4 (progressive disclosure) is motivated by token cost but formalized only loosely. A sub-structural or resource-sensitive type system would make token consumption a type-level property: a tool call exceeding the context budget becomes a type error rather than a runtime failure. This connects to work on bounded process calculi and quantitative information flow.

Dynamic schema evolution.

The current model treats schemas as static. Production MCP servers update tool definitions at runtime through versioning and deprecation. Extending the calculus with schema migration operations—and proving bisimulation is preserved under compatible migrations or characterizing when it breaks—is directly relevant to industrial deployment of the framework.

Empirical calibration of Φ\Phi.

Schlapbach (2026) demonstrated that the five principles improve routing accuracy empirically. The information-loss characterization of Φ−1\Phi^{-1} (Theorem 5.2) provides a theoretical explanation. Future work could derive a formal lower bound on routing error as a function of the information dropped by Φ\Phi, then validate the bound against the empirical routing curves of that companion study.

Formal prompt-injection model.

The tool-poisoning prevention result (Section 8) assumes descriptions are fully controlled by the server. A richer threat model in which description fields are partially adversary-controlled (e.g., via retrieval-augmented schema injection) requires an information-flow type system supporting non-interference and taint analysis, connecting process-calculus security to classical declassification frameworks.
